meta.title: Awesome Agentic Capacity Planning
meta.intro: The Workload → Trajectory → Resources → Capacity chain, the papers that document each link, and the open questions. Lanes separate one agent run (execution) from what the platform does around it (orchestration); studies of real workloads sit at the bottom. Click any box to highlight it with everything below it and open its card. Drag to move, scroll or pinch to zoom. Missing a paper, maybe yours? Add it with the + button at the top: no account needed, and once published it also appears in the Awesome list on GitHub.
meta.footer: The paper cards come from two earlier review documents, in French: the W→T→R→C Map and the Orchestration Layer Map. Coded in October 2026, with one main cell and at most two secondary cells per paper, each justified by the card.
meta.subtitle: A living map of research on the infrastructure demand of LLM agents

proximity.label: Core to the goal
proximity.def: Predicts, before or during the run, an infrastructure quantity of an agent trajectory, or measures what a prediction is worth against observation for a capacity decision.

proximity.label: Close
proximity.def: Deals with agents or multi-turn sessions but predicts something else (tokens, next step, success), measures without predicting, or provides a mechanism or a simulator.

proximity.label: Analogous
proximity.def: Not about agents (isolated LLM requests, serverless, workflows, analytics, queueing, theory), with a transferable method.

evidence.label: Production
evidence.def: Evaluated on production traces or a production deployment.

evidence.label: Simulation
evidence.def: Simulation or replay without a complete real system.

evidence.label: Analytical
evidence.def: Model, proof, book or position paper, with no empirical evaluation of its own.

verdict.label: Works
verdict.def: Clear, quantified gain, or accurate prediction, against a baseline.

verdict.label: Partial
verdict.def: Gain in some cases only, modest prediction, or decision value not evaluated.

verdict.label: Weak
verdict.def: The method predicts poorly or fails in the evaluated setting.

verdict.label: Finding
verdict.def: Characterization or measurement, with no method to evaluate.

p000.title: Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale
p000.does: 13.5 million sessions and 3.2 million GitHub Copilot users. Each turn triggers a loop of LLM and tool calls, then the session waits, 80.1% of the time at the median for multi-turn sessions.
p000.keyResult: ROC-AUC of 0.73 for idle time longer than 60 s, versus 0.58 for the previous-idle-time heuristic, and 86 to 90% of idle time captured.
p000.whyProximity: Predicts the idle time of agent sessions from the turn that is ending.
p000.gap: Only predictor of agent idle time in production. Predicts neither calls nor resources, and the gain from hibernation is not measured.
p000.limitation: Client-side telemetry. No server resource is measured and the data are not released.

p001.title: When Agents Disagree With Themselves: Behavioral Consistency as an Uncertainty Signal for LLM Agents
p001.does: 8,000 runs on 4 models. The same task yields 2.3 to 4.2 distinct action sequences over 10 runs, and consistent tasks succeed more often.
p001.keyResult: 2.3 to 4.2 distinct action sequences over 10 runs, and 82 to 87% success for consistent tasks versus 41 to 65% for the others.
p001.whyProximity: Measures the variability of agent trajectories, without any infrastructure quantity.
p001.gap: Quantifies the random share of trajectories at fixed configuration, which RQ1 must separate. No infrastructure quantities.
p001.limitation: Short main task, stateless tools and a single temperature. Single-author preprint.

p002.title: Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness
p002.does: On success, the variance due to the harness is 7.8 times that due to the model, and the model ranking flips in 6 comparisons out of 9.
p002.keyResult: With the model fixed, the harness shifts success by 8.5 to 13 points, versus 2.5 to 5 points for the model with the harness fixed.
p002.whyProximity: Concerns agents, but measures success, not demand.
p002.gap: Justifies including the harness in W. Measures neither steps, nor tokens, nor durations per harness.
p002.limitation: Position paper. Grid of 3 models and 100 tasks without confidence intervals, steps and tokens per harness not reported.

p003.short: Not All AI Agents Are Equal
p003.title: Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics
p003.does: The same bash tool is disk-bound on BigCodeBench, CPU-bound on SWE-bench, and stays light on APPS. Allocating CPU per task reduces latency by 32% on average.
p003.keyResult: The same tool is disk-bound, CPU-bound or stays light depending on the benchmark, and allocating CPU per task reduces latency by 32% on average.
p003.whyProximity: Measures the resources of agent tools per task, without predicting them.
p003.gap: Gives the shape of tool resources per task type, which T→R must parameterize. No prediction from W.
p003.limitation: A single VM, a remote LLM whose outputs are replayed, GPU excluded, allocation decided offline.

p004.title: Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows
p004.does: 24-h Azure trace. Schedulers, orchestrators and runners have distinct CPU profiles, and orchestrators gate every inference and every handoff between agents.
p004.keyResult: Three host roles with distinct CPU profiles in a 24-h Azure trace, and per-role core pools that save 25 to 46% of tool CPU-seconds.
p004.whyProximity: Measures agent resources in production, without prediction.
p004.gap: Only production measurement of an orchestration role for agents. No cost per message or per state.
p004.limitation: The orchestrator is measured as an aggregate role, with no cost per message or per state. Trace not released.

p005.title: How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? Analyzing and Predicting Token Consumption in Agentic Coding Tasks
p005.does: SWE-bench Verified with 8 models. Tokens vary strongly from one run to another, and the agent poorly estimates its own consumption before acting.
p005.keyResult: Pearson correlation of 0.04 to 0.39 between predicted and consumed tokens, with systematic underestimation, at a cost of 0.05 to 2.29 times the task.
p005.whyProximity: Predicts an agent’s consumption before the run, but in tokens rather than calls or resources.
p005.gap: Shows that self-estimation is not enough to predict demand before the run. Predicts tokens, not calls or resources.
p005.limitation: One harness and one benchmark. Only tokens and dollars are measured.

p006.title: Efficient Interactive LLM Serving with Proxy Model-based Sequence Length Prediction
p006.does: A small model predicts, before generation, the response length of a large LLM, and the scheduler serves short responses first.
p006.keyResult: Class accuracy of 0.615, and completion time reduced by 30.5 to 39.6% versus FCFS, against 43.7 to 58.2% for an oracle.
p006.whyProximity: Isolated LLM requests, without agents or tools.
p006.gap: Prediction method before execution, at the scale of a single call. Isolated requests, without tools or state.
p006.limitation: Workshop paper. Isolated requests without tools or state, responses capped at 512 tokens.

p007.title: AgenticCache: Cache-Driven Asynchronous Planning for Embodied AI Agents
p007.does: For simulated robots, takes the next action from a cache of frequent sequences and lets the LLM confirm or correct it in the background.
p007.keyResult: Versus synchronous execution, success +22%, latency −65% and tokens −50% on average, but 11.11% success instead of 100% on one benchmark.
p007.whyProximity: Predicts the next action of agents, not their resource demand.
p007.gap: Action sequences are regular enough for a sequence model. Simulators only, with no resource cost.
p007.limitation: Simulators only, structured tasks, no GPU cost measured.

p008.title: Act While Thinking: Accelerating LLM Agents via Pattern-Aware Speculative Tool Execution
p008.does: Learns from past traces which tool call follows which sequence of calls, and launches these calls ahead of time on free resources.
p008.keyResult: Top-1 up to 27.8% and top-3 of 43.9%, mean latency up to −43.5% and P99 up to −55.4%.
p008.whyProximity: Predicts an agent’s next tool, not the number of calls or their resources.
p008.gap: Predicts an agent’s next tool from past traces. Predicts neither the number of calls nor their resources.
p008.limitation: Aggregate accuracy, without coverage or rate of discarded speculations. Tools with side effects excluded.

p009.title: Don’t Stop Me Now: Embedding Based Scheduling for LLMs
p009.does: Re-estimates the remaining length during generation from the model’s internal states, and schedules requests accordingly.
p009.keyResult: Mean absolute error 2.66 times lower than BERT on the prompt, and mean latency 1.66 to 2.01 times lower than vLLM with FCFS.
p009.whyProximity: Isolated LLM requests, without agents or tools.
p009.gap: Refines the remaining work during execution, at the scale of one LLM call. No agents or tools.
p009.limitation: One model, one GPU, independent chat requests without tools.

p010.title: Observation, Not Prediction: Conversation-Level Disaggregated Scheduling for Agentic Serving
p010.does: Reasoning at the conversation level replaces hard-to-predict quantities with observable signals, such as the first prompt or KV cache occupancy.
p010.keyResult: P95 of the time to first useful token reduced by 51.08% versus per-turn disaggregation with 10% mispredictions, without SLO violations.
p010.whyProximity: Compares observation and prediction for an agent-serving decision, the question of RQ3.
p010.gap: Measures what observation is worth versus prediction for a serving decision, which RQ3 generalizes. One workload, one small model.
p010.limitation: One workload (SWE-agent), one small model, one machine, and no migration.

p011.title: InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference
p011.does: During a tool call, chooses for each request whether to keep, discard or move the KV cache based on GPU memory waste over time.
p011.keyResult: Sustained throughput 1.25 to 2 times that of vLLM at equal latency, and GPU memory waste of 0.69% versus 27% when discarding the cache.
p011.whyProximity: Decides on inference state during tools, with a simple estimate of their duration.
p011.gap: Keep-or-release decision during a tool call, with an estimate of its duration. Short pauses, without idle time between turns.
p011.limitation: Short contexts (753 to 2,185 tokens), a single server, no SLO.

p012.title: DeltaBox: Scaling Stateful AI Agents with Millisecond-Level Sandbox Checkpoint/Rollback
p012.does: Checkpoint and restore of a sandbox in a few milliseconds, for agents that explore several branches.
p012.keyResult: State management drops from 47 to 77% of execution time to 3 to 6% on tree searches.
p012.whyProximity: Mechanism for the state of agent sandboxes, without prediction.
p012.gap: Makes sandbox checkpointing almost free. Says nothing about the memory held by an idle sandbox.
p012.limitation: No rollback of network I/O, 24 replayed trajectories, memory of an idle sandbox not measured.

p013.title: Histrio: Actor-based programming and correctness guarantees for serverless environments
p013.does: Lists the operations of an actor on serverless functions. Each message costs a state read, then a transaction that writes the state and the outgoing messages.
p013.keyResult: Throughput capped at around 480 requests per second by the database, versus 270 for classic serverless functions.
p013.gap: Lists the orchestration operations to count for an actor. No per-operation cost measured.
p013.limitation: No per-operation cost, in dollars or in resources. Neither LLM agents nor idle time.

p014.title: Characterizing FaaS Workflows on Public Clouds: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
p014.does: The cost of a serverless workflow breaks down into execution, transfers and orchestration, billed per transition, transaction and byte of state.
p014.keyResult: Cost models that track actual costs with an R² of 0.80 to 0.98, and orchestration at 59 to 92% of the cost on Azure at 1 request per second.
p014.whyProximity: Serverless workflows with a known graph, not agents.
p014.gap: Gives the shape of the per-event cost model that T→R must adopt. The number of events is given there by the graph.
p014.limitation: The graph fixes the number of transitions in advance. Neither LLMs nor long waits.

p015.title: Nalar: A Serving Framework for Agent Workflows
p015.does: Manages the session state of agents in a per-node store, which the runtime places, reuses and migrates along with the KV cache, under two-level control.
p015.keyResult: P95 and P99 reduced by 34 to 74% versus Ayo, CrewAI and AutoGen on a financial-analysis workflow.
p015.whyProximity: Agent serving, but without demand prediction.
p015.gap: Makes session state explicit and mobile. Measures neither the cost of a migration nor the size of the state.
p015.limitation: Migration cost and state size not measured, a single 8B model family.

p016.title: SageServe: Optimizing LLM Serving on Cloud Data Centers with Forecast Aware Auto-Scaling
p016.does: On production traces, decides routing, the number of GPU VMs and model placement from forecast traffic.
p016.keyResult: Up to −25% GPU-hours versus the current deployment and −80% GPU-hours wasted by autoscaling, in simulation on production traces.
p016.whyProximity: LLM fleets with aggregate demand, without agents.
p016.gap: Complete demand-to-capacity chain for an LLM fleet. Demand is an aggregate rate, without sessions or chained calls.
p016.limitation: Results in simulation. Aggregate demand in tokens, without sessions or chained calls, and forecast accuracy not measured.

p017.title: Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems. Queueing Theory in Action
p017.does: Queueing formulas, including Pollaczek-Khinchine for the M/G/1, which relate service variance to waiting time, with setup times and SRPT scheduling.
p017.keyResult: Pollaczek-Khinchine relates the mean waiting time of an M/G/1 to the second moment of the service time.
p017.gap: Justifies predicting the variance of demand and not only its mean. Servers without state or batching.
p017.limitation: Poisson arrivals, independent services, servers without state or batching.

p018.title: AgentServeSim: A Hardware-aware Simulator for Multi-Turn LLM Agent Serving
p018.does: Multi-turn serving simulator that preserves turn order, tool pauses and KV cache residency.
p018.keyResult: Mean error on program duration between −4.79% and +4.70% versus vLLM on three GPUs.
p018.whyProximity: Takes agent trajectories as input, without predicting them.
p018.gap: Takes the trajectory as input and returns capacity, exactly downstream of our prediction. Simulates neither the CPU nor the memory of tools.
p018.limitation: One trace and two dense models. Tool pauses are replayed, without tool CPU or memory cost.

p019.title: Ernest: Efficient Performance Prediction for Large-Scale Advanced Analytics
p019.does: Predicts the run time of a large-scale job from a few well-chosen small runs.
p019.keyResult: Time predicted within 12% for most MLlib jobs and within 20% for GenBase and TIMIT, with a training overhead under 5%.
p019.gap: Transfer method from small runs, to update after a change of model or harness. Not agents.
p019.limitation: Regular Spark jobs. Only execution time is predicted.

p020.title: TraceLab: Characterizing Coding Agent Workloads for LLM Serving
p020.does: Normalizes 4,265 Claude Code and Codex sessions into requests, steps and tool calls, and splits time into generation, tools and human think time. An idealized sweep of the eviction timeout quantifies the prefix cache during pauses.
p020.keyResult: Human think time at 92.3% of session time, tool calls longer than one minute at 4.9% of calls and 92% of tool time, and 95.7% of input tokens served by the prefix cache.
p020.whyProximity: Characterizes steps, tools and pauses of real agent sessions, without prediction.
p020.gap: Public trace to calibrate steps, tools, durations and human pauses, and shape of the KV to keep for an idle agent. Predicts nothing, without physical resources or sandbox.
p020.limitation: 43 developers, the authors’ own research usage, two harnesses. Client-side delays, idealized cache and costs taken from public API prices.

p021.title: From LLM Inference to Agentic Workloads: Characterization and Implications for Serving Systems
p021.does: Instrumented testbed of 10 agent applications, with a per-operation trace and container and GPU telemetry, plus 24 h of production traces. Tools and environment dominate or co-dominate latency in 5 applications out of 10.
p021.keyResult: The median production session is active only 20% of its lifetime, and offloading the sandbox during long LLM calls brings the mean memory of Mini-SWE down from 35.3 to 7.7 GB.
p021.whyProximity: Measures agent resources and idle time on a testbed and in production, without prediction.
p021.gap: Supports the hypothesis of idle but live agents and gives an instrumentation model for measuring T→R. No predictor or sizing.
p021.limitation: Production limited to 24 h and three applications, without a predictor. Sandbox offloading is a testbed proof of concept, excluding human pauses.

p022.title: Rethinking AI Cloud Infrastructure for Agentic Serving Systems with the Aries Experimentation Framework
p022.does: Instruments serving, sandboxes and harnesses with events correlated per trajectory. Tools account for 13 to 48% of latency, and an analytical replay quantifies the trade-off between keeping a sandbox idle and suspending it.
p022.keyResult: With 25 GB of KV cache, more than 176 classic requests fit in memory versus 40 agent requests, and a zero keepalive reduces instance cost by 65% but multiplies total cost by 4.9.
p022.whyProximity: Measures inference and sandbox resources of agents and quantifies suspension, without prediction.
p022.gap: Schema of events correlated per trajectory, a possible format for T traces, and quantification of the keep-or-suspend trade-off. Neither prediction nor orchestration cost.
p022.limitation: One model, one GPU, 20 tasks per benchmark. Suspension costs estimated by replay on the AWS Lambda pricing grid, and production trace without per-step time.

p023.title: The Cost of Dynamic Reasoning: Demystifying AI Agents and Test-Time Scaling from an AI Infrastructure Perspective
p023.does: Measures latency, LLM calls, tokens, KV cache and GPU energy of five agent designs under different budgets, versus ShareGPT. Tool-using agents make 9.2 times more LLM calls than CoT.
p023.keyResult: LATS makes 71.0 LLM calls per request, the prefix cache multiplies the throughput of ReAct by 5.62, and energy per request is 62.1 to 136.5 times that of ShareGPT at 70B.
p023.whyProximity: Measures LLM calls, KV cache and energy of agents by design and budget, without predicting.
p023.gap: Orders of magnitude per agent design and evidence that design and budget belong to W. Neither a trajectory predictor nor tool CPU resources.
p023.limitation: One GPU type and one model family, academic benchmarks with light tools. Tool resources not measured, only their latency.

p024.title: Towards Understanding, Analyzing, and Optimizing Agentic AI Execution: A CPU-Centric Perspective
p024.does: Profiles five agents whose tools run on CPU, then proposes COMB, which overlaps CPU and GPU phases through micro-batches, and MAS, which schedules a mix of tool-using and pure-LLM requests. The tool can account for up to 89% of latency.
p024.keyResult: COMB divides P50 latency by 1.7 in an isolated batch, and MAS divides that of pure-LLM requests by 2.37 versus FCFS, without degrading tool-using requests.
p024.whyProximity: Measures the CPU of agent tools and schedules accordingly, without prediction.
p024.gap: Makes the ratio of CPU cores per GPU a capacity parameter, since the CPU saturates before the GPU. Neither memory, nor iterations per task, nor a predictive model.
p024.limitation: Two nodes, models of 32B at most, synthetic load, neither memory nor state. Ceilings calibrated empirically per machine, without a model that predicts them.

p025.title: Agentic AI Workload Characteristics
p025.does: Correlates Claude Code trajectories in Harbor with vLLM traces, turn by turn, for two models and five benchmarks. With an ideal cache, the LLM takes 71 to 98% of the time, mostly in decode.
p025.keyResult: Prefix cache hit rate of 84.6 to 99.5%, decode at 91.0 to 98.6% of LLM time, and 18.0 turns on ADE for Gemma thinking versus 108.8 in Instant.
p025.whyProximity: Characterizes turns, tools and inference cost of coding agents, without prediction.
p025.gap: Shows that model and mode are first-order W parameters and that cost depends on cache retention. Without concurrent load or KV cache memory.
p025.limitation: Ideal cache without eviction, a single harness, two open models and no concurrent load. Neither KV cache memory nor tool CPU.

p026.title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
p026.does: Profiles 10 agent memory systems by phase (construction, retrieval, generation), with calls, tokens and GPU telemetry. For the same history, total calls range from 300 for BM25 to 19,230 for A-Mem.
p026.keyResult: BM25 reaches 47.0% accuracy for 4,128 J per correct answer, versus 27.7% and 185,873 J for Letta, and construction dominates the energy of LLM-mediated systems.
p026.whyProximity: Measures the cost of memory writes of long-horizon agents, without prediction.
p026.gap: Orders of magnitude of an agent’s memory writes, and token cost super-linear in the history for Letta, A-Mem and MIRIX. Neither dollars nor idle time.
p026.limitation: One node, one local model for the main table and five samples from one benchmark. Neither dollar cost, nor concurrency between users, nor idle time.

p027.title: Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling (BATS)
p027.does: Shows the web-search agent its remaining tool budget (Budget Tracker), then adds planning and self-verification (BATS). With Gemini-2.5-Pro, BATS reaches 24.6% on BrowseComp versus 12.6% for ReAct.
p027.keyResult: Budget Tracker at budget 10 matches ReAct at budget 100 (12.8 versus 12.6%) with 40.4% fewer searches and a 31.3% lower cost.
p027.whyProximity: Shows that a visible budget changes the number of tool calls of agents, without predicting.
p027.gap: Shows that the budget changes the shape of T and not only its bound, and provides a unified cost formula. Neither latency nor tool CPU.
p027.limitation: Mostly web search, uniform tool price set by the authors. Budget in tool calls only, without measured latency or CPU.

p028.title: The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation
p028.does: Full factorial design of 3 harnesses, 2 models and 50 Terminal-Bench Pro tasks. With the model fixed, the harness varies tokens per resolved task by a factor of about 40, at a nearly equal number of turns.
p028.keyResult: Tokens per resolved task of 28k and 37k for Goose versus 1.15M and 1.55M for OpenCode, about 40 times, versus 1.0 to 1.3 times between models.
p028.whyProximity: Measures the effect of the harness on the tokens of coding agents, not on calls or resources.
p028.gap: Justifies including the harness in W for tokens, at a nearly equal number of turns. Missing: LLM and tool calls, cached share and sandbox time.
p028.limitation: One run per combination and 50 tasks, asymmetric caps. The factor of 40 rests partly on a Goose total without an input/output breakdown.

p029.title: The Harness Effect: How Orchestration Design Sets the Token Economics of Enterprise Agentic AI
p029.does: Sets up a cost model in which cumulative input becomes quadratic in the number of turns if the history is replayed, then evaluates a harness that attacks each of its terms. Cost per task −41% versus the old loop.
p029.keyResult: Cost per task drops from $0.21 to $0.12, tokens from 14.2k to 8.8k and median latency from 48 to 27 s, at equal quality according to the authors.
p029.whyProximity: Token cost model of agents by harness, without predicting calls or resources.
p029.gap: Provides a form of cost model, cumulative input quadratic in turns, to be weighted by the cache. Turns, tool calls and orchestration cost not measured.
p029.limitation: Both harnesses come from Writer, which evaluates its own work, and the baseline is run once on 22 tasks. Turns per task not published.

p030.title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation (HAL)
p030.does: Standardized evaluation harness that distributes tasks over hundreds of VMs and logs every LLM call. 21,730 runs on 9 models and 9 benchmarks, ranked by accuracy and dollar cost.
p030.keyResult: On Online Mind2Web, SeeAct with GPT-5 Medium costs $171 and Browser-Use with Claude Sonnet 4 $1,577 for a 2-point accuracy gap, and more reasoning does not help in 21 cases out of 36.
p030.whyProximity: Measures the effect of W on the accuracy and cost of agents, without resources or prediction.
p030.gap: Public logs of 2.5 billion tokens to fit per-factor W→T laws. Neither CPU, nor memory, nor sandbox time, nor variance across repetitions.
p030.limitation: Usually one run per configuration, latency not representative according to the authors. Cost in API prices only, without CPU, memory or sandbox.

p031.title: SWE-Effi: Re-Evaluating Software AI Agent System Effectiveness Under Resource Constraints
p031.does: Re-ranks 15 scaffold–LLM pairs on 50 SWE-bench Verified issues by the accuracy obtained per budget of tokens, dollars, local CPU time and normalized inference time. The best pair changes with the resource.
p031.keyResult: Agentless with Qwen3-32B leads in accuracy (48%) and tokens, AutoCodeRover with Qwen3-32B in CPU time, and an issue failed by SWE-agent with GPT-4o-mini consumes 8.8M tokens versus 1.8M for a resolved issue.
p031.whyProximity: Measures CPU time, calls and tokens of coding agents by scaffold and model, without predicting.
p031.gap: Separates local CPU time from inference time, and gives an affine per-call latency reusable for T→R. Neither memory, nor GPU, nor variance.
p031.limitation: 50 issues, no repetition or variance. Inference time modeled from GPT-4o-mini alone, and neither memory nor GPU measured.

p032.title: Sherlock: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Workflow Execution
p032.does: Places the verifiers of an agentic workflow with a topological policy derived from fault injections, chooses the verifier with a learned selector, and speculates downstream during verification. Accuracy +18.3% versus execution without verification.
p032.keyResult: Accuracy +18.3% versus execution without verification, verification cost −26.0% versus Aflow, and execution time reduced by 51.4 to 62.9% versus blocking verification.
p032.whyProximity: Verification and speculation mechanism for agent workflows, without predicting demand.
p032.gap: Shows that the volume of the trajectory depends on failures and gives a formula for the expected cost of lost work. DAGs from a planner, without loops or GPU memory.
p032.limitation: DAGs produced by a planner, not loops with an unknown number of iterations. Small models on one server, without GPU memory or utilization per node.

p033.title: Reducing Cost of LLM Agents with Trajectory Reduction (AgentDiet)
p033.does: After each step, a cheap LLM rewrites an earlier step of the trajectory to remove useless, redundant or stale information, while sparing the prefix cache. Input tokens reduced by 39.9 to 59.7%.
p033.keyResult: Input tokens reduced by 39.9 to 59.7% and total cost by 21.1 to 35.9%, reflection included, for a success rate that varies from −1.0 to +2.0 points versus the same agent without reduction.
p033.whyProximity: Mechanism that reduces the tokens of coding agents, without predicting calls or resources.
p033.gap: Shows that context management is a harness parameter that changes T, with orders of magnitude for a coding trajectory. Neither latency nor GPU time.
p033.limitation: One harness, two proprietary LLMs and two issue-fixing benchmarks. Cost in API prices only, without latency or GPU time.

p034.title: Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents
p034.does: Logs 1,350 in-context objects across 55 trajectories of a coding agent, then compares two semantic working-memory policies with FIFO, LRU-D and UC. Tool outputs make up 55.5% of the volume.
p034.keyResult: Tool outputs make up 55.5% of the volume, OA removes 1.633 repeated calls per task versus FIFO in calibration but not elsewhere, and GA adds 285 importance calls for about 190 main calls.
p034.whyProximity: Measures the working memory of coding agents and the work of managing it, without predicting.
p034.gap: Four-level scheme for instrumenting a trajectory, and evidence that context management adds calls. No valid success, no GPU cost, no public traces.
p034.limitation: 8 complete blocks, one run per task and per arm, dominated by SymPy. Calibration gains do not transfer to the other repositories.

p035.title: Workload Modeling for Computer Systems Performance Evaluation (Feitelson)
p035.does: Methods for modeling a workload, including heavy-tailed distributions, locality of sampling and goodness-of-fit tests. Chapter 8 proposes a three-level user-centric model: population, sessions and activity within the session.
p035.keyResult: For Unix process durations, the tail is heavy with α close to 1, so a process that has already run for t should run for another t.
p035.whyProximity: Non-LLM workload modeling, a method transferable to agent trajectories.
p035.gap: Gives the shape of a hierarchical generator (user, session, loop, calls) and heavy-tail tests. No LLM data and no T→R step.
p035.limitation: Examples predate LLMs. No method for a loop in which each iteration depends on a stochastic model, nor for linking an event to its cost.

p036.title: Speculate While You Reason: Teaching Agents to Predict Their Next Tool Call via Joint Agent–Speculator RL
p036.does: The same model predicts its next tool call, tool and arguments, and launches it while it reasons. After SFT then RL, the exact call is guessed in 61.2% of cases, versus 29.1% by prompting.
p036.keyResult: Exact call guessed in 61.2% of cases after RL, versus 44.1% after SFT and 29.1% by prompting for Qwen3-4B, with no loss of success (26.4 then 27.7%).
p036.whyProximity: Predicts an agent’s next tool call, not the number of calls or their cost.
p036.gap: An agent guesses its own call better than a smaller draft model, but 34 to 39% of speculative executions are discarded. No remaining calls, no cost.
p036.limitation: Only one step ahead and 4-billion-parameter agents. Neither end-to-end latency nor the cost of discarded executions is measured.

p037.title: Dynamic Speculative Agent Planning
p037.does: A cheap agent proposes steps that the target agent verifies in parallel, and a DistilBERT learned online chooses at each step how many to launch ahead. Total cost −30% at comparable speedup.
p037.keyResult: Versus sequential on OpenAGI, k fixed at 6 saves 25.88% of time for +176.25% cost, and DSP 25.26% for +69.36%, i.e. 60.65% of the extra cost avoided.
p037.whyProximity: Predicts mid-loop the number of steps guessed ahead, not the remaining calls or the resources.
p037.gap: Online predictor on the partial trajectory, transferable to remaining calls, and 3 to 6 simultaneous API calls at peak. No GPU or queue measurement.
p037.limitation: Two benchmarks, and both agents share GPT-4.1-mini except in the DeepSeek variant. API dollars and latency only, without GPU or queueing.

p038.title: Interactive Speculative Planning: Enhance Agent Efficiency through Co-design of System and User Interface
p038.does: A fast agent executes up to 4 steps ahead, which a slow agent verifies in parallel, and everything after the first disagreement is discarded. Total time −20.37 to −42.30% on OpenAGI.
p038.keyResult: Time reduced by 19.18 to 42.30% depending on benchmark and setting, but +71% in dollars in setting 1 of OpenAGI and 4 to 5 simultaneous API calls instead of one.
p038.whyProximity: Speculates an agent’s next steps and quantifies the extra cost, without predicting calls or resources.
p038.gap: Baseline for step speculation, bounded to k + 1 simultaneous calls, with its extra cost quantified. Discarded steps consume tools, with no sandbox measurement.
p038.limitation: Two benchmarks, OpenAI models, no server-side measurement. Discarded steps have already called tools, whose cost is not measured.

p039.title: LLM Agents Already Know When to Call Tools, Even Without Reasoning
p039.does: A linear probe on the hidden state of the prompt’s last token predicts, before any generation, whether the task requires a tool. Prefilling the response removes 48% of tool calls for 1.7 points of accuracy.
p039.keyResult: AUROC of 0.894 to 0.957 in single-hop and 0.80 to 0.97 in multi-hop, and −48% tool calls for −1.7 points, versus −6% for the best prompt.
p039.whyProximity: Predicts before generation whether a tool will be called, not the number of calls or their cost.
p039.gap: The need for a tool can be read from the internal state before generation, in under 1 ms. No number of calls, no cost, no subsequent turns.
p039.limitation: One binary decision per task before generation, with no number of calls, tool choice or subsequent turns. Requires access to hidden states.

p040.title: Hermes: Efficient Serving of LLM Applications with Probabilistic Demand Modeling
p040.does: A probabilistic graph, learned from 1,000 runs per application, gives via Monte Carlo the distribution of the remaining time, tightened at each step. The scheduler ranks by Gittins index and pre-warms KV cache, LoRA and containers.
p040.keyResult: According to arXiv v1, mean completion time −77.0% versus vLLM and −66.7% versus VTC on LLaMA2-7B, and +15.3% without online refinement.
p040.whyProximity: Predicts during the run the remaining time of tool-using LLM applications, refined at each step.
p040.gap: Probabilistic graph, Monte Carlo and Gittins chain reusable for remaining calls. Missing: accuracy as a function of progress, and the cost of state between steps.
p040.limitation: Recurring applications profiled 1,000 times, nothing for a new application. Error on the remaining time not measured, figures from arXiv v1.

p041.title: Beat the Long Tail: Distribution-Aware Speculative Decoding for RL Training
p041.does: In RL, a length class drawn from past rollouts of similar requests, revised according to the length produced, tunes the speculative decoding of each response. Rollout time reduced by more than 50% in math.
p041.keyResult: Rollout time reduced by more than 50% in math and by about 25% in code versus VeRL without speculation, with identical or comparable reward curves.
p041.whyProximity: RL rollouts on isolated responses, without agents or tools.
p041.gap: Predicting a class rather than a number, over a recent window, transfers to remaining calls. Scale of a single LLM call, accuracy not measured.
p041.limitation: Isolated responses without agents or tools, and a gain tied to problems that recur at every epoch. Class accuracy not measured.

p042.title: Latency-Aware Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows on Heterogeneous GPUs
p042.does: A GNN predictor estimates the time, peak memory and loading of each call, propagated over the declared DAG to predict the timing of the next steps. The scheduler prepares what follows and manages replicas, makespan −36.8% at best.
p042.keyResult: Under bursts, makespan −36.8% versus Kairos and −35.8% versus Parrot, but −1.6 to −6.6% versus Kairos under Poisson, and only 1.0 to 3.0% versus GBDT.
p042.whyProximity: Predicts GPU time and memory of the remaining steps of multi-agent workflows, but on a declared DAG.
p042.gap: Shows that a finer predictor yields little, 1 to 3% versus GBDT. Does not handle loops with an unknown number of iterations.
p042.limitation: DAG declared in advance, branches and loops not predicted. Two servers, models of 14B at most and 180 sessions.

p043.title: Real-Time Progress Prediction in Reasoning Language Models
p043.does: Estimates during reasoning the fraction of the trace already written, via a probe on hidden states or via tags that the fine-tuned model writes after each paragraph. MAE of 0.161 at best.
p043.keyResult: Qwen3-4B with masking reaches an MAE of 0.161 in math versus 0.238 for the prefix-over-mean-length baseline, but Qwen3-0.6B does worse than the baseline (0.281 versus 0.226).
p043.whyProximity: Remaining work of a single reasoning call, without agents or tools.
p043.gap: Provides refinement baselines and measures irreducible uncertainty through eight continuations of the same prefix. No tools, no loop iterations.
p043.limitation: A single reasoning call, three small models, mostly math. Normalized progress says nothing about remaining tokens in absolute terms.

p044.title: Predictive Business Process Monitoring with LSTM Neural Networks (Tax et al.)
p044.does: An LSTM predicts, from the prefix of a business-process case, the next activity and its delay, then unrolls until the end of the case. Exact next activity at 76.0% on BPI'12 W.
p044.keyResult: Versus transition systems, the error on the delay of the next event drops by 42% then 6% as the case progresses, and the suffix reaches 0.767 similarity versus 0.252 (Polato et al.).
p044.whyProximity: Human business processes, not agents, but the same problem as remaining calls.
p044.gap: Model form and per-prefix-length protocol reusable for an agent’s remaining calls. No uncertainty, no resources.
p044.limitation: Human processes with delays in days. The LSTM overestimates the remaining time when an activity repeats, a frequent case in an agent loop.

p045.title: Survey and Cross-benchmark Comparison of Remaining Time Prediction Methods in Business Process Monitoring (Verenich et al.)
p045.does: Review of 24 studies and benchmark of 16 methods that predict, at each event, the remaining time of a case, on 16 real logs. The LSTM is the most accurate on 13 of 16 logs.
p045.keyResult: Error relative to the mean case duration of 40% on average for the LSTM, from 0.07 to 0.56 depending on the log, versus 59% for transition systems.
p045.whyProximity: Human business processes, not agents, protocol transferable to remaining calls.
p045.gap: Transferable protocol: temporal split, prefixes up to 20 events and weighted MAE, with XGBoost baselines. Does not predict the number of remaining events.
p045.limitation: Human business processes, whose cases last on average up to 387 days. Target in time, not in number of events.

p046.title: Agentix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs
p046.does: Schedules the LLM calls of agent programs according to the service each program has already received, without predicting anything, and swaps the KV cache to CPU RAM on preemption. Throughput ×4 to ×15 versus vLLM at equal latency.
p046.keyResult: At equal latency, program throughput ×4 to ×15 versus vLLM and ×2 to ×5 versus optimized engines, with 6.66 to 159.7 LLM calls per program on average depending on load.
p046.whyProximity: Prediction-free baseline for agent programs, with the gap to a clairvoyant SRPT, the RQ3 question.
p046.gap: Baseline that observes without predicting, whose gap to oracle SRPT indicates what a remaining-calls predictor can yield. No per-program cost, no sizing under SLO.
p046.limitation: Only LLM calls are scheduled, without tool time or program state outside the GPU. One machine with 8 A100s, synthetic arrivals.

p047.title: Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting
p047.does: Separates the prompt (prefill), compute-bound, and generation (decode), memory-bound, onto distinct machine pools. In simulation, throughput 2.15 times that of Baseline-A100 at equal power and cost.
p047.keyResult: With mixed batching, conversation spends 60 to 70% of the time at 20 active tokens or fewer, and Splitwise-AA gives in simulation 2.15 times the throughput of Baseline-A100.
p047.whyProximity: Independent LLM requests, without chained turns or tools.
p047.gap: Public Azure traces, open-source simulator and piecewise-linear cost model for T→R (inference). Nothing on the chained calls of an agent.
p047.limitation: Independent requests, without chained turns, KV reuse across turns or tool waits. Cluster results taken from the simulator.

p048.title: TrEnv-X: Transparently Share Serverless Execution Environments Across Different Functions and Nodes
p048.does: Shares serverless environments across functions and nodes, through reusable sandboxes and memory images in a CXL or RDMA pool. For some agents, the sandbox reaches 42% of total cost at AWS Lambda pricing.
p048.keyResult: Versus E2B, startup −35 to −49%, P99 up to −58% and memory −61%, for agents of 74 to 1,246 MB and 3.2 to 193.1 s per run.
p048.whyProximity: Measures the cost of agent sandboxes and provides a mechanism, without prediction.
p048.gap: Gives the cost of a sandbox as duration × price × memory, and agent profiles for T→R (tools). Missing the share spent waiting on the LLM, call by call.
p048.limitation: Six agents and a workload built by the authors, cost at AWS Lambda pricing. The share of billed duration spent waiting on the LLM is not measured.

p049.title: PeakBench: Benchmarking Resource-Aware Tool Invocation in LLM Agents
p049.does: Benchmark of 300 workflows over about 1,200 MCP tools profiled for static and dynamic cost. The LLM produces a DAG then a schedule, replayed by a simulator to measure capacity violations.
p049.keyResult: Without profiles, LLMs obtain a CVA of 3.458 to 4.588, versus 5.865 for ASAP and 2.925 for the best classical rule, and profiles reduce it for seven models out of eight.
p049.whyProximity: Resources of agent tool calls under finite capacity, without trajectory prediction.
p049.gap: Tool profile format, static and dynamic cost per resource, and CVA metric for T→R (tools). Links neither billed cost nor LLM calls.
p049.limitation: Concurrent execution replayed by a simulator on three fictitious machines. No link to billed cost or to LLM calls.

p050.title: Orleans: Distributed Virtual Actors for Programmability and Scalability
p050.does: Defines the virtual actor, activated on the first message and deactivated after a period of idle time, with explicit persistence of its state.
p050.keyResult: About 130,000 heartbeats per second on 25 servers, near-linear throughput up to 125 servers and a median latency of 6.5 ms up to 19% CPU.
p050.whyProximity: Actors for interactive services, not agents.
p050.gap: Fixes the lifecycle of an actor that T must count. No cost for activation, deactivation or state writes.
p050.limitation: Technical report without baseline. The measured service does not persist its state, so no write is quantified.

p051.title: Netherite: Efficient Execution of Serverless Workflows
p051.does: Groups durable workflow instances into partitions and commits several steps in a single storage access, with recovery through checkpoint and log replay.
p051.keyResult: Throughput up to 18.6 times that of the original engine, and storage accesses divided by 4.4 to 71.6.
p051.gap: Gives the number of storage accesses per workflow step, the basis of a per-event cost. No per-instance memory, no idle-time cost.
p051.limitation: Figures from the engine’s own team, as factors rather than absolute values, with no dollar cost or per-instance memory.

p052.title: Agentic Workflows are Serverless Applications, so deploy them that way!
p052.does: Overview of serverless hosting of LLM applications. Model loading and initialization still dominate startup latency, and agentic workloads have not been characterized in serverless. Proposes serverless deployment of agents with pre-warming.
p052.keyResult: Model loading and initialization still dominate startup latency in serverless, and the authors find no characterization of agentic workloads in this setting.
p052.whyProximity: Addresses agent deployment, but the content is not verified.
p052.gap: Argument for deploying agents as serverless with pre-warming, layer by layer. No measurement or prediction.
p052.limitation: Position paper based on the abstract, with no quantitative evaluation.

p053.title: Durable Functions: Semantics for Stateful Serverless
p053.does: Formalizes Durable Functions, with activities, orchestrations and entities, and proves exactly-once execution of internal state despite failures and duplicate workers.
p053.keyResult: Theorem 6.4 establishes that the replay model and the compute-storage model are bisimilar, without any measurement of latency, throughput or cost.
p053.gap: Lists the per-work-item operations to count in T for an agent in a durable workflow. No order of magnitude.
p053.limitation: Formal paper without measurements. Replay assumes deterministic orchestration code and a short history.

p054.title: Boki: Stateful Serverless Computing with Shared Logs
p054.does: Exposes to serverless functions a shared log, replicated three times, that carries state, exactly-once workflows and message queues.
p054.keyResult: An exactly-once workflow step costs 3.8 ms versus 19 ms on DynamoDB, and a median append 2.03 ms at 1.2 million operations per second.
p054.gap: Gives unit costs for durable state writes and reads. No CPU, memory or disk per operation.
p054.limitation: Prototype on a dedicated EC2 cluster, without production traces. Costs in latency and throughput, without resources or dollars.

p055.title: SQLite: Past, Present, and Future
p055.does: Compares SQLite with DuckDB on transactional and analytical workloads. In WAL mode, SQLite reaches 10,000 TATP transactions per second for one client on a server.
p055.keyResult: SQLite in WAL mode reaches 10,000 transactions per second for one client on a server, 10 to 500 times DuckDB depending on database size.
p055.gap: Order of magnitude of a durable-state transaction in an embedded database. No isolated fsync, no idle agent state.
p055.limitation: A single client, without concurrent writers. The effect of durability settings is not isolated.

p056.title: Efficient and Scalable Agentic AI with Heterogeneous Systems
p056.does: Per-task cost and latency model of an agent graph, set by the bottleneck resource, and placement of tasks on heterogeneous accelerators under SLA.
p056.keyResult: H100 for prefill and Gaudi 3 for decode approach the TCO of a homogeneous B200 cluster, and a 200 to 400 Gbps link is enough for the KV cache.
p056.whyProximity: Cost model for an agent graph, without trajectory prediction.
p056.gap: Bottleneck-resource cost form, reusable for T→R. Additive, without batching or an unknown number of iterations.
p056.limitation: No validation on a real system. Only the LLM of a voice agent is optimized, and the model remains additive.

p057.title: Workflow Aware Analytical Model to Predict Performance and Cost of Serverless Execution
p057.does: Analytical model that estimates the response time and cost of a serverless workflow, loops and parallel branches included, then searches for the best configuration under a budget.
p057.keyResult: Mean accuracy of 99.2% on response time and 98.7% on cost on AWS Lambda, and of 98.6% and 98.2% on Azure.
p057.whyProximity: Serverless workflows with known structure, not agents.
p057.gap: Known-structure baseline for the cost of a workflow. Assumes as given the number of iterations that W→T must predict.
p057.limitation: Card based on the abstract only. Serverless functions without LLM, and the number of iterations is assumed known.

p058.title: Teola: Towards End-to-End Optimization of LLM-based Applications
p058.does: Turns each request of an LLM application into a graph of primitives, rewrites this graph and schedules its nodes. Latency there is not the sum of the module latencies.
p058.keyResult: Mean end-to-end latency up to 2.09 times lower than the baselines, for an optimization overhead of 1.3 to 3% of latency.
p058.whyProximity: LLM applications with a fixed workflow, without agents.
p058.gap: Shows that costs do not add up along a known graph. Handles neither agent loops nor resources.
p058.limitation: Fixed workflows only, without dynamic agent loops. Latency only, without resource cost.

p059.title: HeraSys: Collaborative Serving of Multiple LLM Workflows via Fine-Grained End-to-End Optimization
p059.does: Serves several concurrent LLM workflows by merging identical nodes across requests and by finely scheduling batches and resources.
p059.keyResult: At concurrency 300, P99 of 63.52 s versus 137.89 s for LangGraph and 94.40 s for Ayo, and throughput up to 1.50 times that of Ayo.
p059.whyProximity: Concurrent agentic workflows, without prediction of their demand.
p059.gap: Quantifies the non-additivity across concurrent workflows, which T→R must model. Short workflows, without idle time or orchestration state.
p059.limitation: One server, one 8B model, short workflows without long agent loops. Neither GPU cost nor orchestration state measured.

p060.title: CLASP: Chained-Request-Aware Scaling and Operator Placement for Serverless Stream Processing
p060.does: Linear per-worker load model that distinguishes local and remote sends, learned online, then scaling and placement of serverless streaming operators.
p060.keyResult: Error on the number of workers below 0.25, throughput up to 2.5 times FaaSFlow and 3.3 times Zhang24, and median latency reduced by 75%.
p060.gap: Gives the form of a placement-dependent message cost, useful for distribution. No LLM, no idle time.
p060.limitation: Homogeneous CPU cluster of 10 workers, short-lived operators, no LLM workload or long idle time.

p061.title: Halfmoon: Log-Optimal Fault-Tolerant Stateful Serverless Computing
p061.does: Two exactly-once protocols for stateful serverless functions, which log only reads or only writes, proven log-optimal.
p061.keyResult: Median latency reduced by 20 to 40% versus Boki and storage divided by 1.2 to 3.4, with a log write taking 1.18 ms at the median.
p061.gap: Gives the cost of a durable state write and a bound on what must be logged. No LLMs, latency only.
p061.limitation: Assumes deterministic functions, so an LLM call would have to be logged separately. Latency only, without CPU or memory.

p062.title: Doing More with Less: Orchestrating Serverless Applications without an Orchestrator
p062.does: Decentralizes orchestration into a library wrapped around each function, with atomic checkpoints in a strongly consistent database.
p062.keyResult: $6.279 per million transitions versus $27.9 for Step Functions, and applications 1.35 to 9.0 times cheaper and up to 2.2 times faster.
p062.whyProximity: Serverless workflows with a static graph, not agents.
p062.gap: Quantifies an orchestration transition operation by operation. Static graphs only.
p062.limitation: Static graphs only, so an agent loop decided at runtime cannot be expressed. Neither CPU nor memory measured.

p063.title: ExoFlow: A Universal Workflow System for Exactly-Once DAGs
p063.does: Exactly-once workflow system on Ray, in which per-task annotations set which outputs to checkpoint and when to synchronize.
p063.keyResult: p50 latency about 51% lower than with Beldi on travel reservation, for an exactly-once guarantee that costs about 50% of Ray’s throughput in a microbenchmark.
p063.gap: Shows that the cost of durability is tuned task by task. No LLMs, no idle time.
p063.limitation: No LLM pipeline or idle session. Absolute per-task overhead given only in figures, without dollars.

p064.title: SeBS-Flow: Benchmarking Serverless Cloud Function Workflows
p064.does: Multi-cloud benchmark of serverless workflows that separates function time from orchestration overhead, with their price.
p064.keyResult: On Azure Durable Functions, the overhead of ExCamera is 495.5 s, more than 36 times its critical path of 13.5 s.
p064.gap: Shows that orchestration can dominate the time of a workflow. Graph fixed in advance, without LLM.
p064.limitation: DAG fixed in advance, without LLM or long waits. Orchestration cost estimated on Azure.

p065.title: LogAct: Enabling Agentic Reliability via Shared Logs
p065.does: Makes a durable shared log the substrate of an LLM agent, in which each inference, intention, vote, decision and result becomes a typed entry.
p065.keyResult: 80 KB of log for a 30 s task, i.e. 2.6 KB per second, of which 70 KB is system prompt, and inference dominates the time.
p065.whyProximity: Measures the state written by an agent, without prediction.
p065.gap: Turns the agent’s durable state into a stream of T events. No cost per write.
p065.limitation: No cost per append or per backend, a single 30 s task, no idle time or hibernation.

p066.title: The Hidden Footprint: Making Storage a First-Class Metric for LLM Agent Evaluation
p066.does: The AgentFootprint testbed measures the bytes left on disk per run for eight agent frameworks, and their growth with the number of turns.
p066.keyResult: From 0.32 to 5.10 MB retained per task depending on the framework, i.e. a 15.7-fold gap at equal accuracy, and 323 MB after 200 turns under LangGraph.
p066.whyProximity: Measures the state retained by agents, without prediction.
p066.gap: Shows that W sets the retained state and that it grows with turns. Neither write throughput nor holding duration.
p066.limitation: Bytes retained at the end of the run only, without write throughput, latency or CPU per step. One main model.

p067.title: Crab: A Semantics-Aware Checkpoint/Restore Runtime for Agent Sandboxes
p067.does: To resume an agent after a failure, checkpoints its sandbox only when the turn has actually changed the state, during the next inference. Up to 87% of turns need no checkpoint.
p067.keyResult: Correct resumption in 100% of cases versus 8 to 13% for Chat-only. With an injected failure, total time 0 to 1.9% above the failure-free case, versus 3.06 to 3.78 times for FullCkpt.
p067.whyProximity: Resumption mechanism for agent sandboxes, without prediction.
p067.gap: Shows that more than 75% of turns leave no state to save. Missing: checkpoint size, storage, and memory of an idle sandbox.
p067.limitation: Trajectories replayed deterministically, one failure per task, a single host type. Neither checkpoint size nor storage cost.

p068.title: Memory Compression for High-Fanout Agent Sandboxes (AgentZip)
p068.does: Compresses agent sandbox memory page by page while sandboxes wait for the LLM, and prefetches pages before they are requested. Up to 8.7× less memory for a 1.40× slowdown in Parallel Rollout.
p068.keyResult: In Parallel Rollout, memory −88.55% for a 1.403× slowdown, versus −51.24% and 1.517× for KSM+zswap. In Generate-and-Filter, −64.29% but 1.468× versus 1.118 for zswap.
p068.whyProximity: Mechanism for the memory of waiting agent sandboxes, without predicting idle time.
p068.gap: Memory × time of waiting sandboxes divided by 2.8 to 8.7 at 1.40 to 1.47× the duration. MB per sandbox and the CPU cost are missing.
p068.limitation: Traces replayed on one host, one model and ten Python repositories. The gain relies on sibling sandboxes, and an isolated interactive session is not evaluated.

p069.title: Serverless in the Wild: Characterizing and Optimizing the Serverless Workload at a Large Cloud Provider
p069.does: Characterizes the Azure Functions workload from July 15 to 28, 2019, then tunes keep-alive and pre-warming per application from the histogram of its idle times. 45% of applications are invoked at most once per hour.
p069.keyResult: With a fixed 10 min, 50.3% cold starts at the 3rd quartile, about 2.5× more than the hybrid at equal memory. On OpenWhisk, memory −15.6% and P99 −82.4%.
p069.whyProximity: Stateless serverless functions, not agents, but a transferable retention policy.
p069.gap: Per-entity retention baseline based on its own idle times, with a public trace of real idle times. Nothing on stateful sessions or the KV cache.
p069.limitation: Idle time known to the minute, simulator with identical memory and zero-duration execution. Stateless functions, with no context or sandbox to restore.

p070.title: Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
p070.does: Keeps an agent’s KV cache during a tool call, for a duration chosen from that tool’s past durations, and schedules FCFS at program level. Completion time divided by 1.12 to 3.66 in replay.
p070.keyResult: Completion time divided by 1.12 to 3.66 in trace replay and by 8.18 on a real SWE-agent, throughput multiplied by 1.10 to 3.22, for 0.96 to 2.30 ms of scheduler time.
p070.whyProximity: Decides agent KV retention during tools, from each tool’s past durations.
p070.gap: Keep-or-release rule based on the distribution of tool durations, transferable to the sandbox or the actor. Long idle time between user turns is not addressed.
p070.limitation: Only the GPU KV cache is managed, during tool pauses of a few seconds. Assumes that a tool’s past durations represent its next ones.

p071.title: SpecBox: Speculative Sandbox Scheduling for Efficient LLM Agent Serving
p071.does: Predicts the sandbox the agent will request, through keywords in the token stream and a first-order Markov chain, and pre-warms it during inference. P99 latency divided by 2.9 versus on-demand mode.
p071.keyResult: End-to-end P99 latency divided by 2.9 versus on-demand mode, and peak memory −45.9% versus fully reserved, with cumulative preparation under one second.
p071.whyProximity: Predicts an agent’s next sandbox to pre-warm it, not the number of calls or their durations.
p071.gap: Links a next-tool prediction to a decision on sandbox state. Accuracy and wasted pre-warmings are not quantified.
p071.limitation: Workload built from MCPBench, one model via API, one machine, Docker only. Prediction accuracy and wasted pre-warmings not reported.

p072.title: Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Serving for Multi-turn Conversations with CachedAttention
p072.does: Saves each conversation’s KV cache in an HBM, DRAM, SSD hierarchy and reloads it at the next turn, with retention and prefetching guided by the scheduler queue. Hit rate of 71 to 90%.
p072.keyResult: Versus recomputation, TTFT −61 to −87%, prefill throughput multiplied by 2.6 to 7.8 and end-to-end cost −43 to −70%, with 71 to 90% hits.
p072.whyProximity: Multi-turn sessions, but no prediction of when a paused session returns.
p072.gap: Gives the KV size per token and prices per GB-hour to quantify keeping versus recomputing. The time between turns and a prediction of the return are missing.
p072.limitation: ShareGPT replayed with Poisson arrivals, without think time between turns. Nothing predicts when a paused session returns.

p073.title: KVFlow: Efficient Prefix Caching for Accelerating LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows
p073.does: In a multi-agent workflow with a provided graph, propagates a distance in steps to each agent’s next execution, and uses it to evict or prefetch the KV of its fixed prompt. Speedup of up to 2.91× versus SGLang.
p073.keyResult: Speedup of 2.91× versus SGLang and 1.83× versus HiCache on a single workflow, up to 2.19× versus HiCache under concurrency, but 1.08 to 1.12× on PEER.
p073.whyProximity: Multi-agent workflows with a known graph, KV retention without statistical prediction.
p073.gap: The retention signal is a distance in steps, which predicted remaining calls could provide without a graph. Idle durations and memory cost are missing.
p073.limitation: The graph must be static and provided by the framework, which an agent loop does not give. Mostly synthetic workloads, one GPU per testbed.

p074.title: FaasCache: Keeping Serverless Computing Alive with Greedy-Dual Caching
p074.does: Treats keep-alive of serverless containers as a cache, with a Greedy-Dual priority combining frequency, initialization cost and size, and eviction under memory pressure only. On OpenWhisk, 2× more requests served than the 10-min TTL.
p074.keyResult: On the Representative sample, cold-start overhead divided by more than 3 versus TTL between 15 and 80 GB. On OpenWhisk, 2× more requests served and 6× lower latency.
p074.gap: Reusable priority form for keeping an idle sandbox, recency plus frequency × rebuild cost / memory. Session-specific state and idle durations are missing.
p074.limitation: A single server, frequency and size distributions assumed stable. Containers are interchangeable, whereas an agent sandbox carries a session’s state.

p075.title: Resume Means Resume: A Machine-Checked Conformance Contract for Checkpoint, Interrupt, and Resume Semantics in Workflow Persistence Layers
p075.does: Defines in TLA+ six properties that a resume must guarantee after a human interruption or a crash, and tests them on five agent frameworks. No two profiles are identical, and the REMIT sequencer fixes the fork and double consumption.
p075.keyResult: LangGraph replays an effect after a SIGKILL, and two concurrent resumes trigger it twice, in 10 out of 10 repetitions.
p075.whyProximity: Resume in agent frameworks, but correctness only, without cost or latency.
p075.gap: Fixes what an agent resume must guarantee, including an effect executed exactly once. Does not say what a resume costs.
p075.limitation: Correctness only. Neither cost, nor latency, nor checkpoint size is measured.

p076.title: Hibernate Container: A Deflated Container Mode for Fast Startup and High-density Deployment in Serverless Computing
p076.does: Adds a hibernated state between warm container and cold start, in which the suspended process has its memory swapped out, then reloaded on wake-up. Hibernated, it occupies only 7 to 25% of warm memory.
p076.keyResult: Hibernated, the container occupies 7 to 25% of warm memory. With REAP, its first request takes 3 to 67% of the time of a cold start.
p076.whyProximity: Generic serverless containers, not agents, transferable hibernation mechanism.
p076.gap: Quantifies the memory cost and wake-up latency of a sleeping state, a third option between keeping and destroying. No policy, no agent, no disk cost.
p076.limitation: Generic serverless containers, one machine and micro-functions. No policy decides when to hibernate, and the cost of disk and swap-out is not measured.

p077.title: RainbowCake: Mitigating Cold-starts in Serverless with Layer-wise Container Caching and Sharing
p077.does: Splits containers into three layers, Bare, Lang and User, downgraded as TTLs expire, and shares the lower layers across functions. Startup latency −68% and wasted memory −77% versus Pagurus.
p077.keyResult: On OpenWhisk, startup latency −68% and wasted memory −77% versus Pagurus, with a per-layer TTL capped by a break-even threshold.
p077.whyProximity: Serverless containers without their own state, not agents, transferable graduated retention.
p077.gap: Suggests graduated hibernation, with a per-tier TTL capped by a break-even threshold. Session-specific state cannot be shared across agents.
p077.limitation: Containers without durable state. Agent-specific state cannot be shared, and its reloading on wake-up is not modeled.

p078.title: Linear Elastic Caching via Ski Rental
p078.does: Evicts each cache page after B/r seconds, the cost of a miss over the cost of its memory per second, a 2-competitive rule for an isolated page. In Spanner, this TTL is multiplied by a learned factor.
p078.keyResult: In Spanner, −15.5% cache memory and about −5% TCO for +5.5% misses, with TTL = λ·B/r and λ learned between 0 and 2.
p078.whyProximity: Database cache, not agents, retention rule transferable to actors.
p078.gap: Baseline rule for putting an idle actor to sleep, at worst 2× the optimum for an isolated object. Does not predict wake-ups, wake-up cost assumed fixed.
p078.limitation: Fixed and known miss cost, whereas for an agent it depends on the state to reload. Does not predict arrivals.

p079.title: Keep-Alive Caching for the Hawkes process
p079.does: For bursty arrivals modeled by a Hawkes process, keeps the application while the intensity exceeds c_p/c_cs, yielding a TTL that grows with recent activity, and pre-warms when arrivals are regular.
p079.keyResult: On the Azure trace, a gain of about 4.5% on wasted memory for the 25% of applications handled, and of 0.95% across all of them.
p079.whyProximity: Serverless applications, not agents, wake-up rule transferable to actors.
p079.gap: Exact form of a TTL that grows with recent activity, transferable to an actor’s wake-ups. Wake-up cost assumed fixed and small gain on a real trace.
p079.limitation: Constant costs, infinite capacity, a single event stream. Does not distinguish waiting for a tool from waiting for the user, nor the cost of reloading state.

p080.title: Competitive Randomized Algorithms for Nonuniform Problems
p080.does: For spin-block and snoopy caching, waiting until the fixed cost C then blocking is 2-competitive and optimal among deterministic algorithms. Drawing the threshold according to e^(t/C) achieves e/(e−1), about 1.58.
p080.keyResult: Deterministic threshold 2-competitive and optimal, randomized threshold at e/(e−1) ≈ 1.58, and at most e/(e−1) in expectation for a threshold tuned to a known distribution of waits.
p080.gap: Keeping an idle agent until the resume cost, then hibernating it, costs at most 2× the optimum. Only two states, without estimating the idle-time distribution.
p080.limitation: Only two actions, linear and known costs, worst-case guarantees. Nothing on the expected cost under a real workload.

p081.title: Online Strategies for Dynamic Power Management in Systems with Multiple Power-Saving States
p081.does: For a device with several power-saving states, LEA follows the lower envelope of costs and is 2-competitive, and OPBA learns the idle-time distribution from a histogram of recent periods.
p081.keyResult: Energy of 446.45 J for OPBA versus 438.47 J for the optimum, i.e. +1.8%, and 647.41 J for LEA, i.e. +47.7%.
p081.whyProximity: Power management of a disk, not agents, transferable to the states of an idle agent.
p081.gap: Multi-state model, with holding cost and resume cost, for keeping, compressing, snapshotting or destroying. These costs and the idle-time distribution of agents are missing.
p081.limitation: A single disk and a single trace source. Stepping down to a lower state is assumed free, whereas writing a snapshot or moving a KV cache has a cost.

p082.title: Improving Online Algorithms via ML Predictions
p082.does: Adds a prediction to ski rental and to non-clairvoyant scheduling. The parameter λ sets the trade-off between consistency 1 + λ if the prediction is correct and robustness 1 + 1/λ otherwise.
p082.keyResult: With prediction, the deterministic algorithm beats the classic randomized one as long as the standard deviation of the error stays at most 2b, and PRR never does worse than round-robin.
p082.whyProximity: Theory of online algorithms with prediction, not agents.
p082.gap: Turns an idle-time predictor into a guaranteed keep-or-hibernate policy. Intermediate states, measured costs and an error in distribution are missing.
p082.limitation: A single idle period, known linear costs, error in absolute distance. Synthetic validation only, without multiple states or capacity.

p083.title: Learning-Augmented Dynamic Power Management with Multiple States via New Ski Rental Bounds
p083.does: Gives, for ski rental with prediction, an optimal (ρ, μ) trade-off between competitive ratio and sensitivity to error, then extends it to multi-state power management through k parallel ski rentals.
p083.keyResult: Cost at most (1 + ε) times the best ρ·OPT + μ(ρ)·η, plus an additive term, i.e. about the optimum at zero error and 1.58× at worst.
p083.whyProximity: Theory of power management with prediction, not agents.
p083.gap: Form of a multi-state agent lifecycle policy, each state with a holding cost and a rebuild cost. These measured costs and the wake-up latency are missing.
p083.limitation: Randomized algorithms only, linear costs, totally ordered states. Wake-up counts as a cost, not as a latency under SLO.

p084.title: FleetOpt: Analytical Fleet Provisioning for LLM Inference with Compress-and-Route as Implementation Mechanism
p084.does: Sizes two GPU pools, short and long context, each viewed as an M/G/c queue whose servers are the KV slots, and compresses prompts just above the boundary. Up to −82.4% GPU cost versus a homogeneous fleet.
p084.keyResult: GPU cost −82.4% on Azure and −57.6% on LMSYS, but only −6.7% on the agentic workload, and utilization underestimated by 0.1 to 2.7% versus the simulator.
p084.whyProximity: LLM fleets with independent requests, the agentic workload being only a synthetic length distribution.
p084.gap: Reusable R→C form, from lengths and throughput to GPUs via an M/G/c queue, where the utilization cap, not the SLO, sets the size. Lengths given, not predicted.
p084.limitation: Preprint marked work in progress, validated only against the authors’ simulator and on utilization. Poisson arrivals, one model-GPU pair, synthetic agentic workload.

p085.title: Optimizing Deployment Configurations for LLM Inference
p085.does: A simulator fed by more than 100,000 operator microbenchmarks per hardware explores hardware, runtime and parallelism, and selects the configuration with the best throughput under TTFT and TTIT caps. Simulated latencies within ±5% of measurements.
p085.keyResult: Simulated latencies within ±5% of measurements, ×1.5 to ×2.2 QPS for the disaggregated runtime versus continuous batching, and about 30% of capacity saved by migrating most services to it.
p085.whyProximity: LLM fleets, where agents appear only as length profiles, without tools or idle time.
p085.gap: Reusable per-operator profiling method for T→R (inference), and industrial agent SLOs, TTFT of 200 to 800 ms. Does not size a fleet for variable demand.
p085.limitation: Steady-state throughput at a fixed batch size, without arrivals, queue or P99. Agents appear only as length profiles, without tools or idle time.

p086.title: PiLLM: Resource-Efficient LLM Inference Using Workload Prediction
p086.does: Forecasts the LLM inference workload to dynamically allocate the number of GPUs and the memory reserved per request, and thereby reduce the double over-provisioning across GPUs and within each GPU.
p086.keyResult: No figures in the part of the abstract that was read, which announces two levers, the number of allocated GPUs and the memory reserved per request.
p086.whyProximity: LLM fleets, with no sessions, tools or orchestration state mentioned.
p086.gap: Links a workload forecast to the number of GPUs and to memory per request. Predictor, conversion and forecast error remain to be extracted from the full text.
p086.limitation: Card based on three sentences of the abstract. Predictor, conversion to GPUs, setup and gains remain unknown, and nothing indicates sessions or tool calls.

p087.title: AdaGen: Workload-Adaptive Cluster Scheduler for Latency-Optimal LLM Inference Serving
p087.does: Cluster scheduler that classifies requests by prefill and decode lengths, balances load and distributes some requests across several instances, guided by a simulator of the compute layout. Up to 3.6× higher SLO attainment.
p087.keyResult: Up to 3.6× higher SLO attainment and 2× better cost-efficiency versus existing systems, not named in the abstract.
p087.whyProximity: Isolated LLM requests in a multi-instance fleet, without agents or tools.
p087.gap: Latency depends on the mix of lengths in each instance, not only on load. The number of instances, the estimator’s error and agents are missing.
p087.limitation: Card based on the abstract alone, without trace, model or estimator error. No sessions, no tool calls, no KV cache reuse.

p088.title: OpScale: Operator-level Provisioning and Autoscaling for LLM Serving
p088.does: Sizes and autoscales each operator of the inference graph rather than the whole model, with an M/M/R queue per operator and a greedy heuristic under SLO. Up to −36.3% GPUs on production traces.
p088.keyResult: Up to −36.3% GPUs and −28% power under SLO versus DynamoLLM, AIBrix and vLLM Production Stack, with a greedy plan at most 8% more costly than the oracle.
p088.whyProximity: LLM fleets with independent requests, without agents or demand forecasting.
p088.gap: Reusable R→C form, from throughput and lengths to GPUs via an M/M/R queue. A demand made of agent loops, with reused context and tools, is missing.
p088.limitation: Non-peer-reviewed preprint that assumes Poisson arrivals and exponential service times, fragile under the bursts of an agent loop. Independent requests, without sessions, tools or KV cache reuse.

p089.title: TokenScale: Timely and Accurate Autoscaling for Disaggregated LLM Serving with Token Velocity
p089.does: Autoscales disaggregated prefill and decode pools by dividing token throughput by the profiled Token Velocity, and absorbs bursts through Convertible Decoders. Up to 14% fewer GPUs on A100 and 47% on H100.
p089.keyResult: SLO met for 89 to 96% of requests versus 62 to 88% on 8B, and a provisioned-vs-needed instance correlation of 0.63 and 0.44 versus 0.51 and 0.21 for DistServe.
p089.whyProximity: LLM fleets with independent requests, without agents, tools or prefix caching.
p089.gap: Gives the conversion of token throughput into instances and an accuracy metric for sizing. Without prefix caching or sessions, it would overestimate an agent’s prefill.
p089.limitation: No prefix caching, so the prefill of an agent whose prompt is mostly cached would be overestimated. Simulated length predictor and independent requests without tools.

p090.title: Murakkab: Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflow Orchestration in Cloud Platforms
p090.does: For declared agentic workflows, a MILP solved every 60 min chooses settings, models, GPU instances and routing from profiles, the EWMA-forecast throughput and the SLOs. Versus LangGraph, 912 GPUs instead of 2,568.
p090.keyResult: Versus hand-tuned LangGraph, 912 GPUs instead of 2,568, or 2,472 with autoscaling, and $47.2k instead of $211.7k or $112.3k.
p090.whyProximity: Predicts before the run, from profiles, the GPU resources of agentic workflows and sizes them under SLO.
p090.gap: Links per-setting token profiles, model throughput and GPU instances, the W→T→R→C chain for workflows. Loops with an unknown number of iterations, sandbox, orchestration state and idle time are missing.
p090.limitation: Profiles amortized only for mostly static workflows, and chat and code traces transposed into workflows. The text does not say whether the results are measured or computed.

p091.title: InferLine: latency-aware provisioning and scaling for prediction serving pipelines
p091.does: Plans offline the hardware, batch size and replicas of each stage of a model pipeline, validated by a simulator under a P99 SLO, then adds replicas online according to traffic envelopes. Planner up to 7.6× cheaper than coarse-grained baselines.
p091.keyResult: On Social Media and the Big Spike trace, 99.8% of requests within the SLO for $8.50, versus 93.7% for $36.30, and 34.5× fewer misses on Slowly Varying.
p091.whyProximity: Stateless ML model pipelines, not agents.
p091.gap: Reusable form, per-stage profiles, simulator and greedy search under P99, then online correction. The cost of a request is fixed, with no W→T model.
p091.limitation: Service time assumed independent of the input, whereas an agent loop has an unknown number of iterations. Requests without state or session, on K80 GPUs.

p092.title: StreamBed: Capacity Planning for Stream Processing
p092.does: Measures on a 48-slot testbed the maximum sustainable throughput of a Flink query, fits a scaling law and inverts it for sizing. The predicted configurations, up to 1,069 task slots, sustain 100% of the requested throughput.
p092.keyResult: Predicted configurations that sustain 100% of the requested throughput, for example 1,069 task slots for q5 at 2.5 million events per second, after 10 to 20 measurements on 48 slots.
p092.gap: Method for sizing a fleet of sandboxes or orchestrators from a reduced testbed. An event has a stable cost there, and the SLO is a throughput, not a latency.
p092.limitation: Throughput SLO only, without latency or variable load. Five Nexmark queries, no baseline, and a fixed 110% margin because the predictions are close to saturation.

p093.title: Rafiki: Task-Level Capacity Planning in Distributed Stream Processing Systems
p093.does: Profiles the maximum capacity of each task of a Flink job, locates the bottleneck through backpressure and derives a capacity table per parallelism level. Capacity underestimated by 5 to 14% or overestimated by 3 to 6% depending on the job.
p093.keyResult: Capacity underestimated by 10.31% on average on Yahoo and overestimated by 5.38% on IoT, based on the measured time to drain a backlog of messages.
p093.gap: Suggests profiling the capacity of each service, LLM, sandbox or storage, then provisioning at a target utilization with a catch-up margin. Continuous stream at stable cost.
p093.limitation: Two jobs, a 3-node cluster, no comparison. No latency, no load forecasting, no rule to go from the table to a configuration.

p094.title: PASCAL: An Architecture for Proactive Auto-Scaling of Distributed Services
p094.does: Forecasts the input throughput with a neural network, converts it into CPU per node through a learned profile, and adds nodes early enough for the migration to finish before the peak. Average MSE of 3% on the forecast.
p094.keyResult: Versus a reactive autoscaler on Storm, 0% lost tuples versus 5.22% under a square-wave load, and a mean latency of 1,259 ms versus 2,944 ms under a sawtooth load.
p094.whyProximity: Stream processing and datastore, not agents.
p094.gap: Anticipates the activation delay, which depends on the data to migrate, analogous to reactivating an agent whose state must be reloaded. Aggregate load and CPU only.
p094.limitation: Four servers in a private cluster, only CPU modeled for Storm, and a single real trace accelerated 60×. Unpredictable peaks not covered.

p095.title: Agile Dynamic Provisioning of Multi-Tier Internet Applications
p095.does: Sizes each tier of a web application with a Kingman G/G/1 bound, combining predictive provisioning about every 15 min and reactive provisioning about every 5 min. Facing a 20× surge, capacity doubles in 5 min.
p095.keyResult: The model meets the target response time where reactive provisioning alone violates the SLA, and switching to a dormant VM takes less than one second versus 40 s to more than 11 min.
p095.gap: R→C form transferable to agent sessions with think time, a per-server queue bound, then slow predictive and fast reactive provisioning. Assumes a stable request cost.
p095.limitation: Homogeneous servers, perfect load balancing and prediction based on daily repetition. No session state to keep between two requests, hence no state-reactivation cost.

p096.title: AutoScale: Dynamic, Robust Capacity Management for Multi-Tier Data Centers
p096.does: Manages the capacity of a datacenter where turning on a server takes about 260 s, through a 120 s delayed shutdown, packing-based routing and a number of servers derived from the requests in the system. About 44% less energy than AlwaysOn under SLA.
p096.keyResult: T95 of 491 ms for 1,297 W, versus 291 ms for 2,323 W with AlwaysOn and more than 7 s for Reactive and Predictive, i.e. about 44% less energy than AlwaysOn.
