p096.gap: Provides the fixed idle-timeout baseline, which meets the SLA without prediction, and sizes on the work in progress. No state to save or restore.
p096.limitation: Short, stateless web requests, a single testbed. Shutting down costs only time and energy, with no application state to save or restore.

p097.title: Resource Central: Understanding and Predicting Workloads for Improved Resource Management
p097.does: When an Azure VM is created, predicts in classes its mean and P95 CPU, its lifetime and the size of its deployment, mainly from the subscription’s history, to oversubscribe servers. Accuracy of 79 to 90%.
p097.keyResult: Accuracy of 79 to 90%, precision of 0.85 to 0.94 with abstention below 0.6 confidence, and in simulation 6× fewer readings above 100% CPU than without prediction.
p097.gap: Shows that the subscription’s history predicts consumption at deployment, with abstention and fallback to the declared allocation. VM granularity, without calls, GPU or idle-time cost.
p097.limitation: Placement gains simulated, as the modified scheduler is not in production. CPU only, VM granularity, without calls or GPU.

p098.title: Take it to the Limit: Peak Prediction-driven Resource Overcommitment in Datacenters
p098.does: Predicts the peak CPU usage of each Borg machine from 10 h of history to admit tasks under overcommitment, and compares the predictors to a peak oracle. More than 16% usable CPU capacity gained in production.
p098.keyResult: On about 24,000 machines over one month, more than 16% additional usable CPU capacity with the max predictor, versus more than 10% for borg-default.
p098.gap: Provides the peak oracle and the violation, severity and savings metrics, and argues for predicting per machine rather than per task. CPU only, with no idle time or state.
p098.limitation: CPU only, 5-min trace and a single one-month A/B test. Long-running serving tasks, with no idle time, no state to preserve and no GPU.

p099.title: A New Approach to Capacity Scaling Augmented with Unreliable Machine Learning Predictions
p099.does: Online algorithm, ABCS, that sets the number of active servers by following an ML prediction of the load, while keeping a worst-case guarantee when the prediction is wrong. Empirical competitive ratio of 1.0 to 1.6 with prediction.
p099.keyResult: Competitive ratio close to 1 + 1/r if the prediction is good and bounded whatever the error, with an empirical ratio of 1.0 to 1.6 versus 1.2 to 2.2 without prediction.
p099.whyProximity: Theory of sizing with predictions, not agents.
p099.gap: Framework for calibrating trust in a predictor of agent work without losing the worst case. The model ignores sessions, state and power-on time, where no bounded ratio exists.
p099.limitation: Fluid model with homogeneous servers and continuous capacity, without power-on time. Prediction provided only once, no sessions or state.

p100.title: Queueing, Predictions, and Large Language Models: Challenges and Open Problems
p100.does: Review of queues with predicted service times, such as SPJF, SPRPT and 1-bit prediction, and of the LLM-serving traits absent from classical models. In M/M/1, SPJF brings the mean response time down from 10 under FIFO to 5.36.
p100.keyResult: Under heavy-tailed service, an exact 1-bit prediction with preemption gives a mean response time of 4.65, versus 29.0 under FIFO and 5.22 under SPRPT.
p100.whyProximity: Queueing theory with predictions and LLM serving, without agent loops.
p100.gap: Gives the shape of an agent turn viewed as a job of predicted size, with bounded error cost, and the choice between keeping, discarding or moving the KV cache. No trace, no orchestration.
p100.limitation: Review with no theorem or measurement specific to LLMs. Single server, Poisson arrivals and synthetic errors, without agent loops or off-GPU state.

p101.title: Scheduling with Predictions and the Price of Misprediction (Mitzenmacher)
p101.does: Exact sojourn time in M/G/1 when the queue orders jobs by predicted sizes (SPJF, PSPJF, SPRPT). The price of misprediction, relative to the same algorithm with exact sizes, is 4/3 for a batch with exponential sizes and predictions, versus 2 without information.
p101.keyResult: In M/M/1 with noisy prediction, mean sojourn time of 5.36 with SPJF versus 4.20 with exact SJF and 10 with FIFO at λ = 0.9, and 29.05 versus 18.45 and 100 at λ = 0.99.
p101.whyProximity: Queueing theory with predicted sizes, not agents.
p101.gap: Judges a predictor by its effect on latency, and a very noisy predictor keeps most of the gain over FIFO. A single server, with no state to keep.
p101.limitation: A single server, i.i.d. jobs, free preemption with no KV cache to keep, and joint actual-predicted distribution assumed known. Synthetic examples only.

p102.title: Notes on Effective Bandwidths (Kelly)
p102.does: Defines the effective bandwidth of a bursty source, additive and lying between mean rate and peak rate, and derives from it a linear admission constraint that bounds the overflow probability by e^(−γ).
p102.keyResult: Without a buffer, P(overflow) ≤ e^(−γ) as soon as Σ n_j·α_j(s) ≤ C − γ/s, and with a buffer the acceptance region is approximated by Σ n_j·α_j(s*,t*) ≤ C + (B − γ/s*)/t*.
p102.whyProximity: Theory of multiplexing bursty sources, not agents.
p102.gap: Provides a per-class demand statistic, between mean and peak, for sizing under a guarantee. No estimator on traces, no coupled resources, no correlated sessions.
p102.limitation: Asymptotic results for independent, stationary sources, a single scalar resource, and α to be recomputed when the mix changes.

p103.title: Benchmarking LLM Serving Systems for Agentic AI Workloads with XPerf
p103.does: Traces an agent application without modifying it, as a DAG of LLM and tool calls with token IDs, then replays it under a different load. The prefix cache hit rate of mini-SWE-agent drops from 91% to under 4% under heavy load.
p103.keyResult: Request-latency MAPE under 3% per application and 1.9% under concurrent load, for tracing that adds 0.1% latency.
p103.whyProximity: Replays agent trajectories to measure serving, without predicting them.
p103.gap: Freezes a trajectory into a DAG of calls and replays it under another load, downstream of our prediction. Tools remain pauses, with no CPU or memory.
p103.limitation: A single engine (vLLM) and a single GPU type, cross-engine replay not demonstrated. Tool durations are replayed, with no CPU, memory or sandbox state.

p104.title: Vidur: A Large-Scale Simulation Framework for LLM Inference
p104.does: Simulates LLM inference operator by operator from profiles on one GPU, then searches for the configuration with maximal QPS per dollar under SLO. The optimum for one trace costs up to 2 times more on another.
p104.keyResult: Error of at most 3.33% under static load, up to 12.65% at 95% load, and search for LLaMA2-70B in about 1 h versus 42,000 GPU hours.
p104.whyProximity: Isolated LLM requests, without agents or tools.
p104.gap: Gives the shape of the T→R (inference) model and a search-based sizing baseline. No sessions, no KV cache across turns, no tools, no idle time.
p104.limitation: Isolated requests, without multi-turn sessions, tools or idle time. Validated against a single engine, a fork of vLLM, on 4-GPU VMs.

p105.title: CherryPick: Adaptively Unearthing the Best Cloud Configurations for Big Data Analytics
p105.does: Chooses the VM type and cluster size for a recurring analytics job, by Bayesian optimization of the cost of a run under a time constraint. A bad choice costs 2 to 3 times more on average.
p105.keyResult: Optimum found in 45 to 90% of cases, otherwise within 5% of its cost at the median, whereas exhaustive search costs 6 to 9 times more in dollars.
p105.gap: Method to size a sandbox or inference pool in a few runs, without a workload model. No transfer across workloads, no interactive load.
p105.limitation: Recurring batch jobs with representative input, a single cloud and 66 configurations. No interactive load, no state across runs, no per-request SLO.

p106.title: PARIS: Selecting the Best VM across Multiple Public Clouds
p106.does: Predicts the mean and P90 performance of a workload on each VM type of a cloud, from its fingerprint on 2 reference VMs and a random forest. Error divided by 2 to 4 compared with the baselines.
p106.keyResult: Relative RMSE of about 9% on latency and 11.21% on throughput with 2 reference VMs, and up to −45% user cost compared with the baseline-based choice.
p106.gap: Shows that a forest trained on reference workloads predicts never-seen workloads from 2 measured configurations. No GPU, no tokens, no idle time.
p106.limitation: Assumes a representative task provided by the user. A single VM without scaling, one fingerprint per cloud, no GPU and no state during idle time.

p107.title: Transfer Learning for Performance Modeling of Configurable Systems: An Exploratory Analysis (Jamshidi et al.)
p107.does: Empirical study of 36 environment changes (hardware, workload, version) on four configurable software systems, to see what transfers from a performance model. Pearson above 0.9 for about a third of the changes.
p107.keyResult: Pearson above 0.9 for about a third of the 36 changes, 0.59 from the noisy Amazon instance, and 72 to 96% of interactions shared between source and target.
p107.whyProximity: Configurable software, not agents, with a transfer method that carries over.
p107.gap: Says what to transfer after a change of hardware, model or harness: a linear shift or the influential options. No measurement cost, no agents.
p107.limitation: Four software systems, only execution time measured, and a single cloud instance, small and noisy. Informal thresholds rather than statistical tests.

p108.title: Matrix: Peer-to-Peer Multi-Agent Synthetic Data Generation Framework
p108.does: Peer-to-peer runtime on Ray actors where each task’s state travels in a serialized message, without a central orchestrator. It sustains 12,400 concurrent workflows on 248 A100 GPUs.
p108.keyResult: Token throughput 2.1 to 15.4 times higher on equal hardware compared with centralized or batch versions, and peak network traffic of about 1 GB/s, 760 MB/s with offloading.
p108.whyProximity: Multi-agent orchestration mechanism, without prediction or per-message cost.
p108.gap: Shows coordinator-free orchestration where state flows in the messages. Measures neither per-message cost, nor queueing time, nor idle time.
p108.limitation: Offline data generation, with no user or idle time. No per-message cost, queueing time or orchestration CPU measured, and state is not durable.

p109.title: Adaptive AI Agent Placement and Migration in Edge Intelligence Systems
p109.does: Places and migrates LLM agents at the edge via LLM-refined ant colony optimization, with a delay and cost model where migration goes through export, transfer, startup and import. Total delay −10.31% and −10.64% compared with the baselines.
p109.keyResult: Compared with Greedy, Polling and Random, total delay −10.31% and −10.64% and resources −38.56% and −49.61% on average, but no term of the model is quantified.
p109.whyProximity: Places and migrates LLM agents, without predicting their trajectory.
p109.gap: Decomposes the cost of an agent migration, a reusable form for placement. No term is measured, no hibernation or KV cache.
p109.limitation: Model terms never quantified, 2-core servers and a single task (CBIR). Refinement LLM not named, no hibernation or KV cache.

p110.title: FAME: QoS-aware Async Service Orchestration for Agentic Workflows (v1: Optimizing FaaS Platforms for MCP-enabled Agentic Workflows)
p110.venue: arXiv 2026 (v3) · preliminary version at IEEE ICWS 2026
p110.does: FaaS middleware for MCP agent workflows that externalizes state and suspends agent and orchestrator via S3 checkpoint and callback during long tools. Under bursty traffic, it costs 8 to 12 times less than VMs.
p110.keyResult: Orchestrator-side cost 2.67 to 8.23 times lower than AWS Durable Functions for long tools, and platform 43 to 106 times cheaper than AWS Bedrock AgentCore under bursts.
p110.whyProximity: Mechanism and cost measurement for agent workflows, without prediction.
p110.gap: Shows that checkpoint-based suspension makes cost independent of the duration of a long tool. No model links the number of events to cost.
p110.limitation: A single cloud (AWS), a few workloads and three runs. Cost aggregated per component, with no model linking the number of events to cost.

p111.title: Substrate-Portable Execution for Production LLM Workflows
p111.does: Compiles five Rufus LLM workflows from a single definition to three targets: in-process, durable (SWF) and batch (Flink). The durable target lengthens duration by 1.1 to 3.4 times, one decision round trip per iteration.
p111.keyResult: No quality difference between targets, all Bradley-Terry intervals including 0, and tokens at about 100% of per-request cost versus under 0.5% for compute, orchestration and messaging.
p111.whyProximity: Measures the share of orchestration in the cost of production LLM workflows, without prediction.
p111.gap: Gives the order of magnitude of orchestration against tokens, under 0.5% of the cost of an active request. Nothing on idle state, dollars or the distribution of iterations.
p111.limitation: One provider, one domain, and a cost given for a representative agent, without dollars. No idle state, sessions or resumption tested.

p112.title: Efficient LLM Serving for Agentic Workflows: A Data Systems Perspective
p112.does: Helium models an agentic workflow as a query plan whose LLM calls are operators, with a proactive cache and cache-aware scheduling that reuse prompts, KV and results across calls.
p112.keyResult: Up to 1.56 times faster than state-of-the-art agent serving systems, on several workloads.
p112.whyProximity: Serving of agent workflows, without predicting demand or resources.
p112.gap: Reuse across calls of a workflow treated as a query plan. The plan is assumed known, with no prediction of calls or resources.
p112.limitation: Card based on the abstract only. The workflow is a known plan, with no tools or sandbox measured.

p113.title: Saving GPU Hours in LLM Inference System Development and Online Workloads with Simulation and DBMS-Inspired Cache Replacement Policies
p113.does: Survey of LLM inference systems centered on cache management, theoretical tools to bound performance, and simulation to analyze a system before building it. Proposes a database-inspired cache replacement policy.
p113.keyResult: The abstract gives no figures. It claims that a database-inspired cache replacement policy substantially reduces GPU hours on online workloads.
p113.gap: Shows that simulation serves to understand an inference system, not only to tune its parameters. Isolated requests, no agents.
p113.limitation: Card based on the abstract only, which gives no figures. Isolated requests, with no agents or tools.

p114.title: Manage the Workloads not the Cluster: Designing a Control Plane for Large-Scale AI Clusters
p114.does: Shapeshifter treats the management of an LLM serving cluster as bin-packing where power, memory and compute budgets abstract the hardware, and continuously readjusts deployments according to observed demand.
p114.keyResult: The abstract reports no results. It proposes managing an LLM cluster as multidimensional bin-packing, continuously rebalanced.
p114.gap: Describes LLM demand over three coupled resources, power, memory and compute, useful for R→C. No measurement, no agents.
p114.limitation: Workshop paper, with no evaluation in the abstract. LLM requests, with no agents or sessions.

p115.title: SuperInfer: SLO-Aware Rotary Scheduling and Memory Management for LLM Inference on Superchips
p115.does: On GH200 Superchips, a proactive SLO-aware scheduler rotates requests, and an engine moves the KV cache between GPU and CPU in duplex over NVLink-C2C.
p115.keyResult: TTFT SLO attainment rate improved by up to 74.7% on GH200, with TBT and throughput comparable to state-of-the-art systems.
p115.gap: Keeping or moving the KV under SLO, transferable to agent pauses. No agent or prediction.
p115.limitation: Specific GH200 hardware, isolated LLM requests, with no agents or tools.

p116.title: AdaServe: Accelerating Multi-SLO LLM Serving with SLO-Customized Speculative Decoding
p116.does: Serves requests with heterogeneous SLOs by building for each one a speculative decoding tree adapted to its latency target, with a pipeline that speculates, selects, then verifies.
p116.keyResult: SLO violations reduced by up to 4.3 times and goodput improved by up to 1.9 times compared with the best baselines.
p116.gap: A single fleet serves different SLOs per request. Nothing on agents or on upcoming demand.
p116.limitation: Isolated LLM requests, with no agents or tools. Card based on the abstract.

p117.title: MICE for CATs: Model-Internal Confidence Estimation for Calibrating Agents with Tools
p117.does: Estimates an agent’s confidence in a tool call from the model’s internal layers, decoded via logit lens and then compared with the final output by a probabilistic classifier.
p117.keyResult: On the STE dataset with Llama3, MICE matches or beats the baselines in calibration error and improves the expected utility of tool calls, with no figure in the abstract.
p117.whyProximity: Tool-using agents, but predicts the correctness of a call, not its cost.
p117.gap: Internal states carry information about a tool call before it is issued. No number of calls, durations or resources.
p117.limitation: A single dataset of simulated tool calls and Llama3 models. Predicts neither the number of calls nor their cost.

p118.title: Speculative Actions: A Lossless Framework for Faster AI Agents
p118.does: Faster models predict an agent’s likely actions, which are executed in parallel and validated only if the prediction is correct. Up to 55% exact prediction of the next action.
p118.keyResult: Up to 55% exact prediction of the next action depending on the domain, with latency reductions that the abstract does not quantify.
p118.whyProximity: Predicts an agent’s next action, not the number of calls or their resources.
p118.gap: Action speculation transferable to tools, with a cost-latency analysis. Discarded branches consume unmeasured calls.
p118.limitation: Games, e-commerce and web search. Neither the latency gain nor the cost of discarded branches is quantified in the abstract.

p119.title: Beyond Prediction: Tail-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference
p119.does: Replaces length prediction with a gamma priority fed by lightweight statistical signals, with cache-aware preemption.
p119.keyResult: On Azure production traces, P99 TTLT 35 to 50% lower than SRPT with perfectly predicted lengths, and TTFT 34 to 47% lower.
p119.whyProximity: Isolated LLM requests, but compares a prediction-free policy with SRPT under perfect prediction.
p119.gap: For the tail, a prediction-free policy beats even an exact prediction, the objection RQ3 must address. Isolated requests.
p119.limitation: Isolated LLM requests, with no agents or tools. Card based on the abstract.

p120.title: AI Agents That Matter
p120.does: Analyzes agent benchmarks and evaluation practices. Accuracy alone makes agents needlessly complex and costly, hence a joint optimization of cost and accuracy.
p120.keyResult: State-of-the-art agents are needlessly complex and costly, and joint optimization reduces cost while maintaining accuracy, with no figure in the abstract.
p120.whyProximity: Concerns agents, but measures cost and accuracy, not resources.
p120.gap: Justifies measuring cost alongside success and keeping held-out sets. No calls, resources or durations.
p120.limitation: Evaluation in dollars and accuracy, without infrastructure resources. The abstract gives no figures.

p121.title: Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction
p121.does: Reduces an entire corpus of agent traces to a minimal finite automaton, used to predict the next step and failure. On twelve public datasets, 7 to 43 states suffice.
p121.keyResult: Automata of 7 to 43 states that replay held-out data with a fitness of at least 0.997, and AUROC up to 0.94 for predicting failure.
p121.whyProximity: Predicts the next step and failure of agents, not the number of calls or their resources.
p121.gap: Compact sequence model, whose structure depends on the harness more than on the LLM. No durations, remaining calls or resources.
p121.limitation: Action structure, without durations or resources. Card based on the abstract.

p122.title: DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec): A Sandbox Infrastructure for Effective Agentic Training at Scale
p122.does: DeepSeek’s production platform for agent training and evaluation sandboxes, with placement, lifecycle, shared memory and on-demand image loading. One unit serves about 3 million sandboxes per day.
p122.keyResult: A unit of about 160 nodes serves nearly 3 million sandboxes per day, more than 380,000 concurrently and more than 5,000 creations per second, and on-demand image loading reduces cumulative disk writes by 57%.
p122.whyProximity: Measures and manages agent sandboxes at large scale, without prediction.
p122.gap: Gives the real scale of agent sandbox demand. No prediction of this demand.
p122.limitation: Report from a single industrial player, focused on RL training. No predictor, rule-based placement.

items.title: Predicting a trajectory, yes. In infrastructure quantities, almost never.
items.body: The families that predict mostly occupy the W→T column, and for agents they mostly predict tokens, the next step or the need for a tool. Four papers predict a quantity close to the goal: the idle time after a turn Copilot in the Wild, the remaining time of recurring LLM applications Hermes, the time and memory of the calls of a declared DAG Latency-Aware Orchestration and the GPUs of declared workflows Murakkab. No family that predicts appears in the tools and orchestration columns.

items.title: Observing already does a lot. That is the objection to address.
items.body: Two of the six papers closest to the goal decide without predicting anything. Observing the conversation reduces P95 by 51.08% versus a per-turn policy that is wrong in 10% of its predictions Observation, Not Prediction, and serving the least-served program first multiplies throughput by 4 to 15 versus vLLM Agentix. A third gains only 1.0 to 3.0% with a predictor finer than a GBDT Latency-Aware Orchestration. In theory, however, a noisy predictor keeps most of the gain versus FIFO Mitzenmacher (ITCS).

items.title: The W configuration matters more than the model.
items.body: With the model fixed, the harness shifts success by 8.5 to 13 points, versus 2.5 to 5 for the model with the harness fixed Stop Comparing, and tokens per resolved task by a factor of about 40 Scaffold Effect. Retained state varies 15.7-fold across frameworks at equal accuracy The Hidden Footprint. These measurements justify predicting from W, but none derives a predictor from them.

items.title: Agent sessions spend most of their time waiting.
items.body: In production, a multi-turn Copilot session is idle 80.1% of the time at the median Copilot in the Wild, and the median session is active only 20% of its lifetime. On a testbed, offloading the sandbox during long LLM calls brings the average memory of Mini-SWE from 35.3 down to 7.7 GB AgentSysBench. The only agent idle-time predictor reaches a ROC-AUC of 0.73, and the gain from hibernation is not measured Copilot in the Wild.

items.title: The predictors validated in production do not target agents.
items.body: They target VMs, machines, functions, caches or business processes. Accuracy of 79 to 90% at VM creation Resource Central, more than 16% of usable CPU Take it to the Limit, about 2.5 times fewer cold starts than a fixed 10 min keep-alive at equal memory Serverless in the Wild, −15.5% of cache memory Linear Elastic Caching. Copilot remains the only exception on agents.

thesis.title: What are the takeaways?
items: Predict, before and during the run, the calls, durations and idle time of an agent trajectory, from W and the prefix.
Translate these quantities into resources per layer, tools and orchestration included, where no prediction exists.
Measure what this prediction yields versus policies that observe.

items.title: Per request, orchestration counts for little. Over time, it holds state.
items.body: Tokens make up about 100% of the cost of an active request, compute, orchestration and messaging less than 0.5% Substrate-Portable Execution. But retained state grows with turns, 323 MB after 200 turns under LangGraph The Hidden Footprint, and on serverless workflows without LLMs orchestration makes up 59 to 92% of the cost on Azure at 1 request per second FaaS Workflows (TPDS).

items.title: Resuming an agent is not a given.
items.body: LangGraph replays an effect after a SIGKILL, in 10 out of 10 repetitions Resume Means Resume. Checkpointing the sandbox when the turn has changed state resumes correctly in 100% of cases, versus 8 to 13% for the Chat-only variant Crab. For durable workflows, resumption is proven without cost measurement Durable Functions.

items.title: Placing agents across machines remains little studied.
items.body: Only four papers address placement, for the session state of agents Nalar, streaming operators CLASP, edge agents Wang et al. and training sandboxes DSec (DeepSeek), and none relies on a prediction of the trajectory. A 24 h Azure trace shows three host roles with distinct CPU profiles, and per-role core pools save 25 to 46% of tool CPU-seconds there Agora (Azure).

nodes.title: Workload: what shapes the trajectory
nodes.html:
Key insights

  • The task alone does not define the workload: the same input yields 2 to 4 paths, and the model, harness or budget shift the whole distribution.
  • The harness often matters more than the model: 7.8× more variance in success, a 40× gap in tokens versus 1.0 to 1.3× between models (2026 preprints), and up to a 9× cost gap between scaffolds for 2 points of accuracy (HAL, ICLR 2026). None measures infrastructure quantities.
  • The budget is a determinant of behavior (BATS), not just an external constraint.
  • Failures probably form a separate regime (costly failures, retries): a success / failure mixture model is plausible.
  • The cost of a step depends on the accumulated history (AgentDiet). Metric to keep: cost per successful task.

What remains open

No parameterized distribution of N_tools, N_LLM, N_loops or tokens as a function of (task, model, harness, budget), no measured termination hazard h(t), and no variance decomposition of infrastructure quantities with repeated runs.

Research questions

RQ1, RQ3

Success metrics
Cost must be reported alongside accuracy. Simple baseline agents match complex agents on HumanEval for much less.
Predictive

nodes.title: Predicting the trajectory
nodes.html:
Key insights

  • The horizon changes everything: during execution, the right next tool comes out as first choice 6 times out of 10; before execution, total tokens are poorly estimated (correlation 0.39).
  • Predictions mostly serve latency (speculation, pre-warming, scheduling), almost never capacity.
  • Uncertainty is often represented (distribution, quantiles) but its calibration is rarely evaluated; Hermes acknowledges this.
  • The “small model for a large one” is an established pattern on the latency side (ISP, AgenticCache, BERT proxy), never used for sizing.
  • No one plots the prediction error of an agent’s remaining work as a function of progress

Open question

No one predicts the number or mix of remaining tool calls per tool class to derive a CPU, memory or sandbox demand from it, nor shows how this prediction sharpens with progress. No one measures what a prediction is worth for a capacity decision.

nodes.title: From trajectory to resources
nodes.html:
Key insights

  • Two families of dimensions: those that add up per event (tokens, sandbox seconds, bytes) and those that depend on the runtime (CPU, memory × time, hibernation).
  • The cost of a fleet is not the sum of event costs: batching, node reuse across workflows, contention and cache hits change it (HeraSys, CLASP, TraceLab).
  • The cost of an LLM call depends on the accumulated context and the cache state, not only on the call itself.
  • The unit cost of orchestration operations (writing state, delivering a message, waking the actor) is measured for stateful workflows (Netherite, Histrio), never for agents.

Open question

No per-layer T->R model for agents. The “embedded databases and serverless that carry state” aspect

Research questions

nodes.title: Keeping and restoring state
nodes.html:
Key insights

  • Break-even: releasing an idle resource pays off only if the idle time lasts longer than restore cost ÷ retention cost per second. Suspending a sandbox as soon as it is idle cuts the instance bill by 65% but multiplies the total cost by 4.9 (Aries).
  • Idle time is partly predictable (Copilot): the decision is made with imperfect predictions.

What remains open

Jointly sizing retention memory, storage and restore bandwidth when several sessions come back at the same time, under a resume SLO. On top of this comes the growth of state with the agent’s age.

nodes.html:
Key insights

  • All assume an already-described demand (length distribution, known workflow, aggregate traffic); none takes as input a distribution of agentic trajectories with tools and state.
  • Prediction plus reactive correction is an established pattern (InferLine, PiLLM, AdaGen, SageServe, PASCAL): it is not a contribution in itself.
  • Small testbed then extrapolation (StreamBed) directly addresses the constraint of a small team.

What remains open

Value of individual versus aggregate information at a fixed SLO; multi-resource capacity that includes sandboxes and persistent state.

nodes.title: Characterization: what traces show
nodes.html:
Key insights

  • Idle time dominates: in production, a coding session is active only 20% of its time at the median (AgentSysBench), with pauses of several minutes between turns (Copilot).
  • Context sets the number of sessions per GPU: with 25 GB of memory for the KV cache, 176 classic requests fit in memory at the same time, versus 40 agent requests, because each agent keeps its whole history. For sizing, context size is what counts, not request rate (Aries).
  • Non-LLM components (tools, orchestration, CPU) often dominate latency and cost (AgentSysBench, CPU-centric, Agora).
  • Tools change over the trajectory (reading then writing), and state grows with the agent’s age (Agent Memory).

Tools and orchestration run mostly on CPU and delay GPU inference; CPU-aware scheduling reduces median latency by up to 1.7×

The same bash() tool is disk-bound on BigCodeBench (~= 200 MB/s, near the ceiling), bound by highly variable CPU on SWE-bench, and stays light on APPS. Context is largely reused from one turn to the next, hence a dependence on a persistent KV cache. Tools change over the trajectory: exploration and reading at first, execution and writing afterwards.
